2.text: Valkaˊʟ̣ên (“having houses of whale’s jaw-bone”), which had during my visit 4 houses with 28 people

3.text: (Register, 7 houses, 39 inhabitants). The underground houses alluded to in the name went

4.text: out of use long ago, and the inhabitants now live in large “genuine houses” of the usual type.¹

5.text: ᴇˊnmɪlɪn (“craggy”), in the Aiˊwan Eskimo language Tɪkɪˊvak, which lies five miles farther on, along

6.text: the shore. It had 17 houses, and a mile from it 2 more, with a total population of 126 (Register,

8.text: Nuˊnlig̣ren (see Plate I, Fig. 2), which had 17 houses in one place, and 4 in another near by, with

10.text: Aˊčon, the last Chukchee village, which had during my visit 5 houses with 24 inhabitants. They

11.text: were very poor Reindeer people, who had turned to seal-hunting as a last resort, but were not

12.text: successful even at that (Register, 4 houses, 19 inhabitants).

14.text: Wuteˊen or Wuˊturen (Eskimo, Čeṛiˊnak), the first Eskimo village, which lies near Cape Ulakhpen.

15.text: It had 8 houses with 58 inhabitants (Register, 14 houses, 77 inhabitants).²

16.text: Between Aˊčon and Wuteˊen, in former times, there was a small settlement, Čeˊnlin, occupied by

17.text: the Wuteˊelɪt and the Chukchee. The greater part of its inhabitants, however, perished in the

18.text: famine of 1880. The remainder turned to reindeer-breeding or emigrated to Wuteˊen and to

20.text: Iˊmtun (Eskimo, Iˊmtuk), a few miles off, which had 12 houses with 65 inhabitants (Register, 9

21.text: houses, 43 inhabitants). Most of the people are Aiˊwan, but four families came from Wuteˊen.

22.text: Iˊᵋen (Eskimo, Ṛɪˊṛak), in Plover Bay, which had only 2 houses with 9 inhabitants (Register, 4

23.text: houses, 24 inhabitants); but two families moved to Euˊnmun a little while before our coming.

24.text: The people are Aiˊwan, and very poor.

25.text: Euˊnmun (Eskimo, Aˊvak), near Cape Chukotsky, which during our visit had 12 houses with 88

26.text: inhabitants. Besides these, two families with 10 men came over from Iˊᵋen, where of late

27.text: sealing has been very unsuccessful. There were then 98 inhabitants in Euˊnmun (Register, 16,

28.text: houses, 101 inhabitants). The people of Euˊnmun are Aiˊwan.

29.text: Čeˊčin (Eskimo, Teˊsik), on the west shore of the bay of the same name (Čečiˊkin quˊim, i. e., Čeˊčin

30.text: Bay),³ which had 18 houses with 94 inhabitants (Register, 25 houses, 142 inhabitants). The

31.text: people are Chukchee and Aiˊwan, half and half.

32.text: Uñiˊin (Eskimo, Uñiˊsak), on Cape Chaplin (Indian Point) (Plate I, Figs. 1, 3), which had 61 houses

33.text: with 442 inhabitants, all of them Aiˊwan (Register, 51 houses, 500 inhabitants).⁴

35.text: Nepeˊkuten (Eskimo, Napaˊkutak), on the island called Ipeˊkut in Chukchee (Eskimo, Ciˊṛluk⁶),

36.text: the last Aiˊwan village: 4 houses, 37 inhabitants (Register, 5 houses, 52 inhabitants).

37.text: ¹ The Chukchee use the expression “genuine house” for a tent-like dwelling with an inner sleeping-room

38.text: made of heavy skins. For description see the chapter on “Habitations,” farther on.

40.text: ³ Mr. Gondatti has confounded Providence Bay with Čeˊčin Bay, which led him to many misunderstand-

41.text: ings, and induced Mr. Bogdanovitch to hint that Mr. Gondatti did not visit all the places that he mentioned

42.text: (BOGDANOVITCH, pp. 66, 67). On the Russian maps Čeˊčin Bay is called Tkachen Bay or Admiral Butakoff’s

43.text: Bay. American whalers call it Marquis Bay, of which Krause made “Marcus Bay.”

46.text: ⁵ Northward from Indian Point my information is reliable only for the number of houses. The Register

47.text: gives the number of inhabitants in every case, but I fear the figures are often only approximate. The average

48.text: of inmates in a house, according to my calculations, which agree with the data given by Mr. Gondatti, is about

49.text: 6½ or 7. Lieut. Nordquist allows for the villages of the Arctic shore not more than 5 to a house, but this

50.text: seems to me rather too little.
